prompt: In MRS GREN, which life process means getting rid of waste made by the body's cells?

options.text: Excretion
Nutrition
Respiration
Sensitivity

feedback.b: Nutrition means taking in or making food.
feedback.c: Respiration releases energy from food. It makes waste carbon dioxide, but getting rid of that waste is excretion.
feedback.d: Sensitivity means detecting and responding to changes in the surroundings.

hints: Examples of this waste are carbon dioxide (breathed out) and urea (in urine).
solution: **Excretion** is getting rid of waste made by cells, such as carbon dioxide and urea. Getting rid of undigested food (faeces) is called egestion. It isn't excretion, because that food was never part of the body's cells.

prompt: In MRS GREN, what does the **S** stand for?
hints: It's about detecting and responding to changes, such as a plant growing towards light or you pulling your hand away from something hot.
solution: **S = Sensitivity**: detecting changes in the surroundings (stimuli) and responding to them.

prompt: Animals that have a backbone are called [[a]].
hints: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals all belong to this group.
solution: An animal with a backbone is a **vertebrate**. Animals without a backbone, such as wētā and earthworms, are invertebrates.

prompt: Match each group of vertebrates to its main features.

right.text: Scales, fins and gills
Smooth, moist skin with no scales
Dry, scaly skin; eggs with leathery shells
Feathers and a beak; eggs with hard shells
Hair or fur; feed their young on milk

hints: Start with the features you are most sure of, such as feathers or fur.
Amphibians, such as frogs, have skin that must stay damp.
solution: Fish → scales, fins and gills. Amphibians → smooth, moist skin. Reptiles → dry, scaly skin and leathery eggs. Birds → feathers, beak and hard-shelled eggs. Mammals → hair or fur, and milk for their young.

prompt: The tuatara looks like a lizard. It has a backbone and dry, scaly skin, and it lays eggs with leathery shells on land. Which group of vertebrates does it belong to?

options.text: Reptiles
Amphibians
Mammals
Fish

feedback.b: Amphibians have smooth, moist skin with no scales.
feedback.c: Mammals have hair or fur and feed their young on milk.
feedback.d: Fish have fins and gills and live in water.

hints: Which group has dry, scaly skin?
solution: Dry, scaly skin and leathery eggs laid on land are features of **reptiles**. But tuatara aren't lizards. They are the only survivors of an ancient group of reptiles that lived alongside the dinosaurs.

prompt: Wētā are insects. Select **all** the features that every adult insect has.

options.text: Six legs
Three body parts (head, thorax and abdomen)
A hard outer skeleton (exoskeleton)
Wings
Eight legs
A backbone

hints: Not every insect can fly.
Spiders are not insects, and insects are invertebrates.
solution: Every adult insect has **six legs**, **three body parts** (head, thorax and abdomen) and an **exoskeleton**. Not all insects have wings. Wētā, for example, have none. Eight legs is a feature of spiders. No insect has a backbone, because insects are invertebrates.

prompt: Species that live naturally in New Zealand and nowhere else in the world are called [[a]]. Species that were brought here by people, such as possums and stoats, are called [[b]].
hints: Native species got here without help from people, but some of them also live in other countries.
solution: **Endemic** species, such as kiwi and tuatara, are found naturally only here. **Introduced** species were brought by people. *Native* is a wider word: native species got here by themselves, and some of them, like the pūkeko, also live in other countries.

prompt: What is the word for the place where an organism lives?
hints: A rocky shore, a stream and a kauri forest are all examples.
solution: A **habitat** is the place where an organism lives. It gives the organism the food, water, shelter and conditions it needs.

| Step | Statement | Go to / name |

| 1a | Has a backbone | Go to 2 |
| 1b | Has no backbone | Go to 4 |

prompt: An animal has a backbone and feathers, but it cannot fly. Use the key to identify it.
hints: Start at step 1 and follow the 'go to' instructions.
Backbone → step 2. Feathers → step 3.
solution: 1a (has a backbone) → go to 2. 2a (has feathers) → go to 3. 3b (cannot fly) → **kiwi**.

prompt: Which pair of statements in the key separates the tūī from the kiwi?

options.text: Statements 1a and 1b
Statements 2a and 2b
Statements 3a and 3b
Statements 4a and 4b

feedback.a: Both the tūī and the kiwi have a backbone, so step 1 sends them the same way.
feedback.b: Both birds have feathers, so step 2 sends them the same way.
feedback.d: Step 4 is only for animals with no backbone.

hints: Follow the key for both birds. Where do their paths split?
solution: Both birds go 1a → 2a → step 3. At step 3 the tūī can fly (3a) and the kiwi cannot (3b), so **statements 3a and 3b** separate them.

prompt: Kiwi have nostrils at the tip of their long beak. This is a [[a]] adaptation that helps them find [[b]] under the ground.
hints: Is this adaptation a body feature, something the bird does, or a process inside its body?
What do kiwi probe the soil for?
solution: It is a **structural** adaptation, because it is a body feature. Kiwi probe the soil with their beak and smell worms and grubs, so it helps them find **food**. Kiwi are the only birds with nostrils at the tip of the beak.

prompt: Match each New Zealand example to the type of adaptation it shows.

right.text: Behavioural adaptation

left.text: Mountain stone wētā can survive their bodies freezing in winter

right.text: Physiological adaptation

left.text: Kākāpō have green feathers that blend in with the forest

right.text: Structural adaptation

hints: Structural = a body feature. Behavioural = something the organism does. Physiological = a process inside the body.
solution: Being nocturnal is something kiwi **do**, so it's **behavioural**. Surviving freezing depends on processes inside the wētā's body, so it's **physiological**. Green feathers are a body feature, so they're **structural**.

prompt: Kai says a fire is alive because it grows, moves, uses oxygen and gives off waste gases. What is the best reason that fire is **not** alive?

options.text: It is not made of cells
It does not move or change position
It does not use any oxygen
It does not get bigger over time

feedback.b: Fire does move as it spreads, so this isn't a good reason.
feedback.c: Fire does use oxygen, as Kai said.
feedback.d: Fire can grow, as Kai said.

hints: Kai's points are all true. Look for something that every living thing has but fire doesn't.
solution: Fire shows some things that look like life processes, but it isn't made of **cells**, and every living thing is. To be alive, something must be made of cells and carry out all seven MRS GREN processes.

prompt: Why does New Zealand have so many endemic species?

options.text: New Zealand has been separated from other land for about 80 million years, so its species evolved on their own
Most of New Zealand's species were brought here by early sailors and settlers
Plants and animals from other countries could easily travel to New Zealand
New Zealand has never had any predators, so its species have never died out

feedback.b: Species brought here by people are introduced, not endemic.
feedback.c: If species could travel here easily, they would also live in other places, so they wouldn't be endemic.
feedback.d: New Zealand had native predators, such as Haast's eagle, and many species, such as the moa, have died out.

hints: Endemic species are found in only one place. What would stop species mixing with those in other countries?
solution: New Zealand split away from the supercontinent Gondwana about 80 million years ago. Because it is so **isolated**, its plants and animals evolved separately from those elsewhere, and many became species found nowhere else.

prompt: Select **all** the species below that are endemic to New Zealand.

options.text: Kiwi
Tuatara
Kauri
Kākāpō
Pūkeko
Brushtail possum

hints: Endemic means found naturally here and nowhere else.
One of these birds also lives naturally in Australia, and one animal was brought here from Australia by people.
solution: Kiwi, tuatara, kauri and kākāpō are found naturally only in New Zealand, so they are **endemic**. The pūkeko is **native**: it got here by itself, but it also lives in Australia and other countries. The brushtail possum is **introduced**: people brought it from Australia in the 1800s.

prompt: Before people arrived, New Zealand's only land mammals were bats. Many New Zealand birds, such as kiwi and kākāpō, are flightless. Explain why flightless birds could survive here, and why they are now in danger from introduced mammals such as stoats and rats.
modelAnswer: There were no mammal predators hunting on the ground, so birds did not need to fly to escape danger. Flying uses a lot of energy, so over many generations, birds that fed and nested on the ground survived and reproduced well without flying. When people brought mammals such as stoats, rats and cats, these predators hunted on the ground, often at night and by smell. Flightless birds can't fly away from them, and their eggs and chicks on the ground are easy to reach, so many are killed.

rubric.criterion: States that there were no (or very few) predators on the ground, so flying wasn't needed to escape
Explains that flying uses a lot of energy, or that ground-living birds survived and reproduced without flying over many generations
Explains that introduced predators hunt on the ground, and flightless birds (or their eggs and chicks) can't escape them

hints: Why do most birds fly? Think about escaping danger.
How and where do stoats and rats hunt?
solution: No ground predators meant flight wasn't needed, and flying costs a lot of energy, so flightless birds survived well. Introduced mammals hunt on the ground, so flightless birds, and their eggs and chicks, can't escape.

prompt: When a kākāpō senses danger, it freezes and stays completely still, and its green feathers blend in with the plants around it. This worked well against its natural predators, such as Haast's eagle, but it doesn't protect kākāpō from stoats. Why?

options.text: Its natural predators were birds that hunted by sight, but stoats hunt mainly by smell
Stoats are much bigger than the eagles that once hunted kākāpō
Kākāpō have lost the ability to freeze since stoats arrived
Stoats only hunt in the daytime, when kākāpō are easy to spot

feedback.b: Stoats are small. Haast's eagle was the largest eagle known to have lived.
feedback.c: Kākāpō still freeze when they are threatened. Adaptations don't disappear within a few lifetimes.
feedback.d: Kākāpō are nocturnal, and stoats hunt by day and by night. The problem is how stoats find their prey.

hints: Camouflage and keeping still fool one particular sense.
How does a stoat find its prey?
solution: Staying still and being camouflaged works against predators that hunt **by sight**, like Haast's eagle and other birds of prey. Stoats hunt mainly **by smell**, and kākāpō have a strong, musty smell, so freezing doesn't hide them.

prompt: Scientists sort organisms into groups that get smaller, with members that are more and more alike. Put these groups in order from the **largest** to the **smallest**.
hints: Kingdom is the largest group, and species is the smallest.
In a scientific name, the genus comes just before the species.
solution: Kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species. A memory aid: **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ood **S**oup.

prompt: A wētā (an insect) and a spider are both arthropods. How many more legs does an adult spider have than an adult wētā?
hints: How many legs does every insect have?
Spiders belong to a group called arachnids. How many legs do they have?
solution: Insects have 6 legs and spiders have 8 legs, so a spider has $8 - 6 = 2$ more legs.

prompt: Archey's frog is one of New Zealand's native frogs. It lays its eggs in damp places on land, not in water, and its young skip the free-swimming tadpole stage. A student says this means it should be classified as a reptile. Explain why it is still classified as an amphibian.
modelAnswer: Scientists classify organisms using many features, not just one. Archey's frog has smooth, moist skin with no scales, and it can take in oxygen through its skin. These are amphibian features. Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and lay eggs with leathery shells, but Archey's frog's eggs have no shell. They are covered in jelly and must stay damp. So even though it doesn't lay its eggs in water, most of its features match amphibians, not reptiles.

rubric.criterion: Gives an amphibian feature the frog has (e.g. smooth, moist skin with no scales; breathing through its skin; eggs with no shell)
Gives a reptile feature the frog does not have (dry, scaly skin or leathery-shelled eggs)
Explains that classification is based on many shared features, not on one feature such as where eggs are laid

hints: Compare the frog's skin and eggs with the features of reptiles.
Do scientists classify using one feature or many?
solution: Archey's frog has moist, scaleless skin and shell-less eggs, which are amphibian features. It has none of the key reptile features (dry, scaly skin and leathery eggs). Classification uses many features together, so it is an amphibian.

prompt: Ana says, "Plants don't do respiration, because they don't breathe." Which statement best corrects her?

options.text: All living cells, including plant cells, respire to release energy from food. Breathing just moves air in and out.
Plants only respire at night, when it is too dark for them to photosynthesise.
Plants breathe in through their roots, so they are able to respire.
Plants don't need any energy, so it doesn't matter that they don't respire.

feedback.b: Plants respire all the time, day and night.
feedback.c: Plants don't breathe. Gases enter plants by diffusion, which isn't the same as breathing.
feedback.d: Plants need energy to grow, reproduce and carry out their other life processes.

hints: Respiration and breathing are not the same thing.
Which life process releases energy inside every living cell?
solution: **Respiration** is a chemical reaction that releases energy from glucose inside cells, and every living cell does it, including plant cells. **Breathing** is just moving air in and out of the lungs. Plants don't breathe, but they respire all the time.

prompt: The scientific name of the North Island brown kiwi is *Apteryx mantelli*. The rowi (Ōkārito kiwi) is *Apteryx rowi*. What does this tell you about these two birds?

options.text: They are different species in the same genus, so they are closely related
They are the same species, because their names start with the same word
They belong to different genera, because the second words are different
They are not related, because scientific names are chosen at random

feedback.b: The first word is the genus. The second word names the species, and these are different.
feedback.c: The genus is the first word, and both birds share it.
feedback.d: Scientific names show relationships. Organisms in the same genus are closely related.

hints: In a scientific name, the first word is one level of classification and the second word is another.
solution: A scientific name has two parts: the **genus** first, then the **species**. Both birds are in the genus *Apteryx*, so they are closely related, but they are different species.

prompt: A kākāpō is a large, flightless, green parrot with a short, hooked beak. What would this key identify a kākāpō as? Explain why, and describe how you would change the key so it can identify both the kiwi and the kākāpō.
modelAnswer: A kākāpō has a backbone (1a → go to 2), feathers (2a → go to 3) and cannot fly (3b), so the key would wrongly identify it as a kiwi. This happens because the key has no statement that separates two flightless birds. To fix it, change 3b to "Cannot fly → go to 5" and add a new step: 5a "Long, thin beak with nostrils at the tip → kiwi" and 5b "Short, hooked beak → kākāpō".

rubric.criterion: Follows the key correctly (1a, 2a, 3b) and states that it identifies the kākāpō as a kiwi
Explains that the key has no step that separates the two flightless birds
Adds a new pair of opposite statements, based on a clear physical feature (e.g. beak shape), that leads to kiwi and kākāpō

hints: Work through the key for the kākāpō step by step.
A new step needs two opposite statements about a feature you can see.
solution: 1a → 2a → 3b gives **kiwi**, which is wrong. The key needs one more step after 3b, for example: 5a long, thin beak with nostrils at the tip → kiwi; 5b short, hooked beak → kākāpō.

prompt: A kōwhai tree grows seed pods full of seeds. Which life process (from MRS GREN) is this?

options.text: Reproduction
Growth
Nutrition
Excretion

feedback.b: Growth means getting bigger. Making seeds is about producing new plants.
feedback.c: Nutrition is getting or making food. Seeds are how the tree produces offspring.
feedback.d: Excretion is getting rid of waste made by the cells. Seeds aren't waste: they grow into new kōwhai trees.

hints: What will the seeds grow into?
solution: Seeds grow into new kōwhai trees, so making seeds is **reproduction**: producing offspring.

prompt: What is the name for an animal that does **not** have a backbone?
hints: Insects, worms, spiders and snails are all examples.
solution: An **invertebrate** has no backbone. Most animal species on Earth, such as wētā, worms, spiders and pāua, are invertebrates.

prompt: Match each life process in MRS GREN to its meaning.

right.text: Changing position, or moving part of the body
Releasing energy from food
Detecting and responding to changes around it
Getting permanently bigger
Producing offspring
Getting rid of waste made by the cells
Taking in or making food

hints: Respiration and excretion are the two that are most often mixed up. One is about energy, the other about waste.
solution:
- **M**ovement: changing position, or moving part of the body
- **R**espiration: releasing energy from food
- **S**ensitivity: detecting and responding to changes
- **G**rowth: getting permanently bigger
- **R**eproduction: producing offspring
- **E**xcretion: getting rid of waste made by the cells
- **N**utrition: taking in or making food

prompt: The pūkeko is a **native** bird in New Zealand, but it is **not endemic**. What does this tell you about the pūkeko?

options.text: It arrived in New Zealand naturally, and it also lives naturally in other countries
It was brought to New Zealand by people, in the same way as the possum
It lives naturally in New Zealand and is found nowhere else in the world
It used to live in New Zealand, but now it is found only in other countries

feedback.b: A species that was brought here by people is **introduced**, not native.
feedback.c: That describes an **endemic** species, such as the kiwi.
feedback.d: A native species lives here naturally now. Pūkeko are common in New Zealand wetlands and farmland.

hints: Native species arrived without help from people.
Endemic species are found in one place only.
solution:
**Native** means it lives here naturally, without having been brought by people. **Not endemic** means it isn't found only here: pūkeko also live naturally in Australia.

Every endemic species is native, but not every native species is endemic.

prompt: Pekapeka (bats) are New Zealand's only native land mammals. They can fly, like birds. Why are they classified as mammals, not birds?

options.text: They have fur and feed their young on milk
They are active at night and rest during the day
They have a backbone and a pair of wings
They catch and eat insects while they are flying

feedback.b: Being active at night is a behaviour, not a body feature used for classifying. Ruru (morepork) are birds that are active at night too.
feedback.c: Birds also have a backbone and wings, so these features don't show that bats are mammals.
feedback.d: Many birds, such as pīwakawaka (fantails), also catch insects in flight. What an animal eats isn't used to classify it.

hints: Think about their body covering, and how they feed their young.
solution: Mammals have **hair or fur** and **feed their young on milk**. Pekapeka have fur and feed their babies milk, so they are mammals. Their wings are made of skin stretched between long finger bones, not feathers.

stem:
Ana found some invertebrates under logs in a Waikato forest. She used this dichotomous key to identify them.

| Step | Statement | Go to / name |
|---|---|---|
| 1a | Has legs | Go to 2 |
| 1b | Has no legs | Go to 5 |
| 2a | Has 6 legs | Wētā |
| 2b | Has more than 6 legs | Go to 3 |
| 3a | Has 8 legs | Spider |
| 3b | Has more than 8 legs | Go to 4 |
| 4a | Has 14 legs (7 pairs) | Slater |
| 4b | Has more than 14 legs | Centipede |
| 5a | Has a shell | Snail |
| 5b | Has no shell | Earthworm |
prompt: Ana finds an animal with a hard, grey body and 14 legs. Use the key to identify it.
hints: Start at step 1 and follow the "Go to" instructions.
At each step, choose the statement that is true for this animal.
solution:
1a (has legs) → 2b (more than 6 legs) → 3b (more than 8 legs) → 4a (14 legs) → **slater**.

Slaters are crustaceans that live on land, in damp places such as under logs.

prompt: The wētā, spider, slater and centipede all have a hard outer skeleton (exoskeleton) and jointed legs. Which group of invertebrates do they **all** belong to?

options.text: Arthropods
Insects
Arachnids
Molluscs

feedback.b: Only the wētā is an insect. Insects have exactly 6 legs and three body parts.
feedback.c: Only the spider is an arachnid. Arachnids have 8 legs.
feedback.d: Molluscs, such as the snail, have soft bodies and no jointed legs.

hints: Insects and arachnids are smaller groups inside one much bigger group.
The name of the big group means "jointed foot".
solution: All four are **arthropods**: invertebrates with an exoskeleton and jointed legs. Arthropods are divided into smaller groups, such as insects (wētā, 6 legs), arachnids (spiders, 8 legs), crustaceans (slaters) and myriapods (centipedes).

prompt: Kahu suggests replacing step 4 with **4a: Is small** and **4b: Is large**. Explain why this would be a poor pair of statements for a dichotomous key.
modelAnswer: "Small" and "large" aren't clear-cut. There is no fixed size that separates them, so two people could make different choices for the same animal. Size also changes as an animal grows, so a young centipede might be smaller than an adult slater and be identified wrongly. Good key statements use clear features that anyone can observe or count in the same way, such as the number of legs.

rubric.criterion: Explains that 'small' and 'large' are not clear or exact, so different people could choose differently for the same animal
Explains that good statements use a fixed feature that can be clearly observed or counted (e.g. number of legs), or that size changes as an animal grows

hints: Would everyone agree on whether an animal is 'small'?
Think about a young animal compared with an adult of a different kind.
solution: A good dichotomous key uses statements with only one possible answer for each organism. Whether an animal is 'small' or 'large' depends on opinion and on the animal's age, so the key could give different answers for the same animal. Counting legs gives the same answer every time.

prompt: Mushrooms grow out of the ground and can't move, like plants. Why are they classified as **fungi**, not plants?

options.text: They have no chlorophyll, so they can't make their own food by photosynthesis
They only grow in dark, damp places, where plants can't grow
They aren't alive, so they can't belong to the plant kingdom
They are made of just one cell, but plants have many cells

feedback.b: Plenty of plants, such as ferns and mosses, grow well in dark, damp places. Where something grows doesn't decide its kingdom.
feedback.c: Fungi are alive: they grow, respire, reproduce (using spores) and feed.
feedback.d: Mushrooms are made of many cells. Some fungi, such as yeast, are single-celled, but that isn't why fungi aren't plants.

hints: How does a plant get its food? Can a mushroom do the same?
solution: Plants contain **chlorophyll** and make their own food by photosynthesis. Fungi have no chlorophyll. They feed by releasing enzymes onto dead or living material and absorbing the nutrients. Their cell walls are also made of a different substance (chitin, not cellulose). So fungi are put in their own kingdom.

prompt: A horse and a donkey can mate and have a foal called a mule, but mules are almost always infertile (they can't have offspring of their own). What does this tell you?

options.text: Horses and donkeys are different species
Horses and donkeys are the same species, because they can mate
Mules are a new species, halfway between horses and donkeys
Horses and donkeys belong to different kingdoms

feedback.b: Being able to mate isn't enough. Members of the same species produce offspring that are **fertile**.
feedback.c: Mules can't reproduce, so they can't form a population of their own. They aren't a species.
feedback.d: Horses and donkeys are both animals, and they are closely related: they are in the same genus, *Equus*.

hints: Think about what the definition of a species says about the offspring.
solution: A **species** is a group of organisms that can breed together and produce **fertile** offspring. Horses and donkeys can produce mules, but mules are infertile, so horses and donkeys are **different species**. They are still closely related: both belong to the genus *Equus*.

prompt: Select **all** the vertebrates.

options.text: Tuatara
Pekapeka (long-tailed bat)
Īnanga (a native fish)
Hochstetter's frog
Wētā
Pāua
Kina

hints: Vertebrates have a backbone.
Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are all vertebrates.
solution:
**Vertebrates:** tuatara (reptile), pekapeka (mammal), īnanga (fish) and Hochstetter's frog (amphibian).

**Invertebrates:** wētā (insect), pāua (mollusc) and kina (echinoderm) have no backbone.

prompt: Match each group of invertebrates to its main features.

right.text: Six legs and three body parts
Eight legs and two body parts
Hard exoskeleton and two pairs of antennae; most live in water
Soft body that is not segmented, often with a shell
Soft body divided into ring-shaped segments

hints: For the groups with jointed legs, count the legs.
Two of the groups have soft bodies. Only one of them is divided into rings.
solution:
- Insects: six legs, three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen)
- Arachnids: eight legs, two body parts
- Crustaceans: hard exoskeleton, two pairs of antennae, mostly live in water
- Molluscs: soft, unsegmented body, often with a shell
- Annelids: soft body made of ring-shaped segments

stem:
Year 9 students surveyed a rocky shore near Kaikōura. They recorded these animals and their main features.

| Animal | Main features |
|---|---|
| Pāua | Soft body; one large, flattened shell; a big muscular foot that grips the rock |
| Kina | Round body covered in hard spines; rows of tiny tube feet; body built in five matching parts |
| Cushion star | Rough, spiny skin; rows of tiny tube feet; five short arms |
| Rock crab | Hard exoskeleton; ten jointed legs, including two claws |

prompt: Molluscs are one group of invertebrates. Which animal in the table is a mollusc?
hints: Snails and mussels are molluscs. Which animal in the table is built most like them?
solution: **Pāua** are molluscs. Like snails, they have a soft body, a single shell and a large muscular foot.

Pāua and kina

feedback.b: Pāua and kina live on the same rocks and both eat seaweed, but sharing a habitat or food doesn't make animals related. Their body features are very different.

prompt: Pāua and kina live on the same rocks and both graze on seaweed. Explain why scientists still classify them in **different** groups.
modelAnswer: Pāua have a soft body, a single shell and a muscular foot, so they are molluscs. Kina have hard spines, tube feet and a body built in five parts, so they are echinoderms, like the cushion star. Scientists classify organisms by their shared body features, because these show how closely related they are. Where an animal lives and what it eats don't show this: very different animals can share the same habitat or food.

rubric.criterion: Describes the features that make pāua a mollusc (soft body, single shell, muscular foot)
Describes the features that make kina an echinoderm (spines, tube feet, five-part body), or links kina with the cushion star
Explains that classification is based on shared body features, not habitat or diet, because unrelated animals can share a habitat or food

hints: Compare the body features of the two animals in the table.
Does living in the same place mean two animals are related?
solution: Classification is based on **body features**, not on habitat or diet. Pāua (soft body, one shell, muscular foot) are **molluscs**. Kina (spines, tube feet, five-part body) are **echinoderms**. They happen to live and feed in the same place, but their bodies are built in completely different ways.

prompt: A dry bean seed in a packet doesn't seem to move, grow or feed. Describe how you could show that the seed is alive, and explain how your result would show this.
modelAnswer: Plant the seed in damp soil (or put it on wet paper towels) and keep it somewhere warm. If it is alive, it will germinate: a root and a shoot will start to grow. Growth is one of the life processes (MRS GREN), so this shows the seed is alive. (Another good test: soak some seeds and check for respiration, for example carbon dioxide turning limewater cloudy, or the seeds warming up.) A dry seed is dormant: its life processes are happening very slowly until it gets water.

rubric.criterion: Describes a valid test: giving the seed water and warmth (e.g. planting it in damp soil) to see if it germinates, or testing soaked seeds for respiration (e.g. carbon dioxide or a temperature rise)
Explains that growth (or respiration) is a life process, so observing it shows the seed is alive

hints: What does a seed need to start growing?
Which MRS GREN process could you then observe?
solution: Give the seed water and warmth, for example by planting it in damp soil. If it germinates and grows, it is alive, because **growth** is a life process. A dry seed is **dormant**, not dead: its life processes are just very slow until it gets water.

prompt: A dichotomous key is used to identify 8 different New Zealand birds. Each step in the key is a pair of statements that splits a group into two smaller groups. How many steps (pairs of statements) does the key need?
hints: Try a smaller example first. How many steps do you need to identify 2 birds? What about 3 birds?
Each step turns one group into two, so the number of groups goes up by one.
solution:
Each step splits one group into two, so each step adds **one** more group. You start with 1 group (all 8 birds) and finish with 8 groups (one bird each). That takes $8 - 1 = 7$ steps.

In general, a dichotomous key for $n$ organisms has $n - 1$ pairs of statements.

prompt: Select **all** the features that **every** mammal has.

options.text: Feeds its young on milk
Has hair or fur at some stage of its life
Breathes air using lungs
Has a backbone
Gives birth to live young
Lives on land
Has four legs for walking

hints: Think about unusual mammals, such as whales, dolphins, bats and the platypus.
A feature only counts if there are no exceptions.
solution:
Every mammal feeds its young on milk, has hair at some stage, breathes with lungs and has a backbone.

The others all have exceptions:
- The platypus and echidnas **lay eggs**.
- Whales and dolphins, such as Hector's dolphins, **live in water**.
- Bats have wings, and whales and dolphins have flippers, instead of **four walking legs**.

stem:
The brown kiwi is a flightless bird found only in Aotearoa New Zealand. Here are some of its features:

- It sleeps in a burrow, a hollow log or thick plants during the day, and feeds at night.
- It has strong, muscular legs with sharp claws.
- Its nostrils are at the tip of its long beak, and it has an excellent sense of smell.
- The female lays an egg that can be up to about one-fifth (20%) of her body mass.
- Its feathers are loose and hair-like.
prompt: Sleeping in a burrow during the day and feeding at night is a [[a]] adaptation. Having strong legs with sharp claws is a [[b]] adaptation.
hints: For each feature, ask: is it something the kiwi does, or a part of its body?
solution:
Sleeping by day and feeding at night is something the kiwi **does**, so it is a **behavioural** adaptation. Strong legs and claws are part of its body, so they are a **structural** adaptation.

A physiological adaptation is about how the body works on the inside, such as a mountain stone wētā surviving being frozen.

prompt: Kiwi can't fly and have hair-like feathers, but they are still classified as birds. Which feature shows that a kiwi is a bird?

options.text: It has feathers and lays eggs with hard shells
It has a backbone and breathes with lungs
It is warm-blooded (keeps a steady body temperature)
It lays its eggs on land, in a nest or burrow

feedback.b: All vertebrates have a backbone, and reptiles and mammals breathe with lungs too, so this doesn't show it's a bird.
feedback.c: Mammals are also warm-blooded, so this doesn't separate birds from mammals.
feedback.d: Reptiles, such as tuatara, also lay eggs on land, so this doesn't show it's a bird.

hints: Which feature is found **only** in birds?
Rule out any feature that mammals or reptiles also have.
solution: **Feathers** are found only in birds, and birds lay eggs with hard shells. A backbone, lungs, a steady body temperature and laying eggs on land are all shared with other groups of vertebrates.

stem:
The brown kiwi is a flightless bird found only in Aotearoa New Zealand. Here are some of its features:

- It sleeps in a burrow, a hollow log or thick plants during the day, and feeds at night.
- It has strong, muscular legs with sharp claws.
- Its nostrils are at the tip of its long beak, and it has an excellent sense of smell.
- The female lays an egg that can be up to about one-fifth (20%) of her body mass.
- Its feathers are loose and hair-like.
prompt: Choose **two** of the kiwi's **structural** features from the list. For each one, explain how it helps the kiwi survive or reproduce.
modelAnswer:
Nostrils at the tip of the beak: the kiwi pushes its long beak into soil and leaf litter and can smell worms and grubs underground, so it can find food in the dark without needing good eyesight.

Strong legs with sharp claws: these let the kiwi dig burrows to shelter in, and kick or slash at attackers to defend itself.

(Another good answer is the large egg: the chick hatches big, well developed and already covered in feathers, so it can soon feed itself.)

Because these features help kiwi find food and stay safe, kiwi that have them are more likely to survive and breed.

rubric.criterion: Explains how one structural feature helps (e.g. nostrils at the beak tip let it smell food underground in the dark)

Explains how a second, different structural feature helps (e.g. strong legs and claws for digging burrows and defence; loose, hair-like feathers keep it warm and help it blend in with the forest floor; a large egg means the chick hatches well developed)
Links the features to survival or reproduction (e.g. it finds more food or stays safer, so it is more likely to survive and breed)

hints: Structural features are parts of the body: the beak, legs, egg and feathers.
For each feature, say what the kiwi uses it for, then why that helps it survive.
solution: Pick two body features and, for each, say **what it does** and **why that helps**. For example, nostrils at the tip of the beak help the kiwi find food underground at night, and strong legs and claws help it dig shelters and defend itself. Features that help an animal get food and stay safe make it more likely to survive and reproduce.

prompt: Pōhutukawa often grow on coastal cliffs, where the wind is strong, the air is salty and the soil is thin and dry. Their leaves are thick and leathery, with a waxy, shiny upper surface and a layer of fine white hairs underneath. Explain how these leaf features help the tree survive in this habitat.
modelAnswer: In strong, dry, salty wind, leaves lose water quickly by evaporation, and the thin soil holds little water to replace it. The thick, waxy upper surface is waterproof, so less water evaporates through it. The hairs underneath trap a layer of still, moist air against the leaf, so the wind can't carry water vapour away as quickly. Thick, leathery leaves are also tough, so they aren't easily damaged by wind and salt spray. Saving water means the tree can survive on a dry, windy cliff.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the problem: wind, salt and dry soil mean the tree could lose water faster than it can take it in
Explains that the thick, waxy surface reduces water loss (evaporation) from the leaf
Explains that the hairs trap still, moist air next to the leaf, reducing water loss, or that tough, leathery leaves resist wind and salt damage

hints: What problem do wind, salt and dry soil cause for a plant?
Think about how each feature could reduce water loss.
solution: The main danger on a coastal cliff is **losing too much water**. The waxy upper surface is waterproof, and the hairs underneath trap moist air so the wind blows less water vapour away. Tough, leathery leaves also stand up to wind and salt spray.

prompt:
Rangi wrote this dichotomous key:

| Step | Statement | Go to / name |
|---|---|---|
| 1a | Has wings | Go to 2 |
| 1b | Has no wings | Go to 3 |
| 2a | Has feathers | Tūī |
| 2b | Has fur | Pekapeka (bat) |
| 3a | Has feathers | Kiwi |
| 3b | Has dry, scaly skin | Tuatara |

Kiwi actually have tiny wings, only a few centimetres long, hidden under their feathers. What would Rangi's key identify a real kiwi as, and what is the best way to fix the key?

options.text: Tūī. Change step 1 to 'Can fly' and 'Cannot fly'.
Pekapeka. Change step 2 to 'Has a beak' and 'Has no beak'.
Kiwi. The key works, so it doesn't need fixing.
Tuatara. Remove step 3 from the key.

feedback.b: A kiwi has feathers, so at step 2 it goes to 2a (tūī), not 2b. The real problem is at step 1.
feedback.c: A real kiwi **has** wings, so it goes 1a → 2a and ends up as a tūī. The key needs fixing.
feedback.d: A kiwi never reaches step 3, because it has wings. It ends up at 2a (tūī).

hints: Follow the key for a real kiwi, remembering that it **does** have wings.
Which feature really separates kiwi and tuatara from tūī and pekapeka?
solution: A real kiwi has (tiny) wings, so it goes 1a → 2a (has feathers) → **tūī**. 'Has wings' doesn't split the animals the way Rangi intended. 'Can fly / Cannot fly' does: tūī and pekapeka can fly, while kiwi and tuatara can't. Then 3a and 3b separate the kiwi from the tuatara.

prompt: Write a dichotomous key that could be used to identify these four animals: **kiwi**, **pekapeka** (long-tailed bat), **tuatara** and **wētā**.
modelAnswer:
| Step | Statement | Go to / name |
|---|---|---|
| 1a | Has a backbone | Go to 2 |
| 1b | Has no backbone | Wētā |
| 2a | Has feathers | Kiwi |
| 2b | Has no feathers | Go to 3 |
| 3a | Has fur | Pekapeka |
| 3b | Has no fur (dry, scaly skin) | Tuatara |

Other keys are also correct, as long as each step is a pair of contrasting statements about one clear feature, and each animal ends up on its own.

rubric.criterion: Each step is a pair of contrasting statements about one feature (e.g. 'Has a backbone' / 'Has no backbone')
Uses clear features that don't depend on opinion (such as backbone, feathers, fur or scales), not size, colour or habitat
Every animal ends up identified on its own, using three pairs of statements

hints: Start with one feature that splits the four animals into two groups.
Keep splitting each group until every animal is on its own. Four animals need three steps.
solution: One possible key: backbone or not (separates the wētā) → feathers or not (separates the kiwi) → fur or scaly skin (separates the pekapeka from the tuatara). Each step uses one clear feature, and every animal ends at its own name.

prompt: Most of New Zealand's native lizards, including our geckos, give birth to live young instead of laying eggs. Geckos have dry, scaly skin and breathe with lungs, and their body temperature changes with their surroundings. A student says geckos should be classified as mammals. Which response is best?

options.text: No. They have scales, not fur, and don't feed their young on milk. Live birth is just one feature.
Yes. Giving birth to live young is the feature that defines a mammal.
No. Their body temperature changes with their surroundings, so they are amphibians.
Yes. Any animal that has lungs and a backbone is classified as a mammal.

feedback.b: Live birth doesn't define a mammal: the platypus lays eggs, and some sharks and lizards give birth to live young. Mammals are defined by having hair and feeding their young on milk.
feedback.c: Amphibians have smooth, moist skin with no scales. A reptile's body temperature also changes with its surroundings.
feedback.d: Reptiles, birds and amphibians also have lungs and a backbone.

hints: Which features do **all** mammals have?
Is one unusual feature enough to move an animal into a different group?
solution: Geckos have dry, scaly skin and no fur, and they don't feed their young on milk, so they are **reptiles**. Classification uses many shared features. Giving birth to live young is unusual for a reptile, but it isn't enough to make a gecko a mammal.
